CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire network security provider Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion.

item.title: University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a .During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.“It is widely promoted as the next step in furthering novel research taking place at this University. What is conveniently left out on flyers and pamphlets is that this is only part of the proposition, 10% in fact, the other 90% is being used by Los Alamos — a nuclear weapons developer,” a sophomore studying biochemistry told the board before the vote. “We already have three existing high tech data centers used for research. Why must we push forward with another one that is promoting nuclear warfare?”An electrician from Ypsilanti Township, a representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) union, supported the construction project. “This will create 300 plus jobs for our members, all local, [and] give back to the community,” he said. “IBEW is in favor of the data center, excuse me, ‘high compute research center.’”People who attended the regent’s meeting to discuss other topics referenced the vote during their presentations. “You voted today to fund a $785 million data center project in Ypsilanti, much to the opposition of the residents of the area, acting against what many residents in the area are calling environmental racism. I think I can speak for many students when I say I am frankly appalled by this decision,” a student who was there to discuss carbon emissions said.A library worker present to talk about how the University treats its workers invoked the data center. “I’m not sure I can confidently appeal to your sense of compassion around this. The officials and residents of Ypsi Township are saying ‘stop,’ saying ‘no,’ saying ‘this hurts.’ And you and others responsible for this nuclear weapons data center project have shown you don’t care about the basic issue of consent as you plow ahead,” he said.Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.Despite the opposition in the room, the regents approved the project. “It’s been very controversial [...] For me, this is all about an investment in the community and it’s an investment, in many different ways,” regent Denise Ilitch said just before the vote. “The community will be enhanced — they may not feel it now, some, but I venture to say that there will be much good that will come from this.”Many in Ypsilanti Township disagree. After the regents voted, the leadership and residents of the Township gathered for a panel discussion about the data center. One of the speakers that night was Jay Coghlan, the executive director of Nuclear Watch of New Mexico, a watchdog group that tracks Los Alamos. “The data center issue here in Ypsilanti is unique in that it is the clearest example of the pending merger of AI and nuclear weapons, which doesn’t bode well,” Coghlan told 404 Media.Coghlan told 404 Media that he shared the Township’s concerns about how the data center will use water and electricity but said he thinks its construction will have farther reaching consequences. “Our nation is transforming from the military-industrial complex that Eisenhower warned us about to a Silicon Valley-Pentagon-Wall Street complex that closely links economics, economic inequality, increasing militarism, and I dare say the rise of techno-fascism,” he said.U of M has repeatedly said the data center will mostly be used to power medical breakthroughs and conduct cancer research, something it’s highlighted in flyers and pamphlets it’s mailed to people in the Township. LANL to the people of the community in September that promised it wouldn't build nuclear weapons in their backyard. “I'm going ‘Duh, yeah, you're not going to bring plutonium to Ypsilanti in Michigan,” Coghlan said. “But I expect this data center to have a lot to do with the design of new nuclear weapons. So, in that way, Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.”Coghlan said he finds hope in the opposition to the project. “I’m very impressed by the intensity of opposition that I have witnessed. There seems to be a pretty widespread public awareness of the data center in Ypsilanti, Township.”During the Township meeting on November 19, after the regents voted, Ypsilanti Township attorney Douglas Winters said he was mad. “What did we learn on November 3rd? Two weeks ago and two days, voters around this country loudly declared that they were sick and tired of government corruption. They were tired of secrecy. They were tired of abuse of power. They were tired of threats to democracy and the disregard of governmental accountability. And, importantly, they also said they were sick and tired of these data centers,” he said. “Somehow that message did not make it to Ann Arbor. That message did not make it to the board of regents.”Winters and other leaders vowed to keep fighting the data center’s construction. In May, the community’s water authority voted to restrict new construction on infrastructure to data center projects while it conducts a review of their impact on the Township’s water supply. The University called the move “unlawfully discriminatory.” In August, the Township passed a six month moratorium on new electrical infrastructure, a move aimed at delaying the project.

item.title: Nvidia Buckles To Trump Pressure, Reinstates Horny, Still Potentially Compromised CEO
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: But Huang’s exodus, while the legally correct move, was starting to seriously disrupt AI and data center investment markets, now bone-grafted to the U.S. economy. The threat of multiple investigations into Nvidia’s financing (and potential infiltration by the Chinese) was jeopardizing Nvidia’s role as the single most-important subsidizing mechanism keeping the AI bubble (and its circular financing) afloat. “NVIDIA today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”Well cool, so glad that’s settled. To start, this is Nvidia openly saying they don’t care about Huang leveraging his authority to have sex with subordinates, something Nvidia employees will likely remember the next time they’re required to sit through workplace sensitivity and ethics training.But more importantly, this is just foundationally from a legal standpoint. There’s been no meaningful investigation into Huang’s long relationship with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang. They have absolutely no idea how compromised Huang’s devices or the Nvidia network is. Nor has anybody even really started digging into Nvidia’s alleged export ban violations or funny financials in Singapore.But worry not! In its statement, Nvidia reiterates that they’ve set up a new commission tasked with making sure it is adhering to export controls and the law (read: there’s no need for pesky government inquiries or deep dives into our finances):“As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.”Despite numerous media outlets credulously insisting last week that the Trump SEC and DOJ were “investigating,” in a statement Donald made it very clear that won’t be happening:How many Trump insiders do you think had early warnings of Huang’s reinstatement and profited off the resulting stock bump?This is not how serious countries function, and this is a dangerous embarrassment. It does, however, speak to how desperate tech titans are to keep the AI industry’s circular financing afloat, which continues to cover up the fact that the lion’s share of large AI companies simply aren’t profitable, and that a massive amount of heavily-debt-addled data center investments likely won’t be completed leaving your retirement money likely holding the bag after the “market correction.”This corrupt and embarrassing capitulation won’t prevent an AI bubble from popping longer term. And while neither Nvidia nor the Trump administration will be particularly incentivized to transparently get to the truth of what happened, a flood of investigations by a reconstituted Congress in the new year is likely to shed all sorts of interesting new details on the entire affair(s) anyway. This is Nvidia very clearly putting the AI hype bubble (and the interests of the extraction class) above ethics, morality, and even national security. It’s utterly clownish, but it’s extremely on par for a country that’s being steadily hollowed out by unethical autocratic corruption.

item.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report: [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. On Sunday night, Nvidia's board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang's reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.
In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang's biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump's key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.
On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia's action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company "made the correct and proper decision." The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Mr. Trump wrote.

item.title: Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You’ll Be the Main Character
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the <user_profile>. The generated customized video follows the style and format of the <top_ watches> of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the <preferred_genres> of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The <top watches> and <preferred _genres> parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says. The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.” The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+. AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea. As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: YC Startup Working On 'Cost Per Kill' For Missiles
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he's not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator's fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. "I think missiles are the coolest thing," Dandzbergs tells WIRED. "A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up."
In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about "attacking hard problems," breaking things down to "first principles," and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war -- a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. "He's a pretty exceptional person," says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. "I'm still somewhat in disbelief that we're talking about a 16-year-old." Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup's guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the "cost per kill." Dandzbergs hopes to demonstrate a prototype missile by December. Despite concerns about the ethical implications of autonomous weapons and his young age, he remains undeterred. "I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare," he says.
"Please don't say I'm sacrificing my childhood," says Dandzbergs. "This is the childhood I dreamed of."

item.title: Teens To Lawmakers: Excluding Us Isn’t The Same As Protecting Us
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: For years and years now we’ve been pointing out that — contrary to popular opinion — the data just doesn’t support the idea that social media is inherently bad for teens. And yet, the media and politicians keep acting as if it’s inarguable. What the data does show is that a very small percentage of teens (somewhere around 3 to 4%) struggle with how much time they spend on social media. And often, social media isn’t the cause of that struggle. Those kids are frequently dealing with other challenges or mental health issues, lack adequate support or treatment, and turn to social media to fill the gap.We’ve long argued that a better approach is to identify those teens and figure out how to get them actual help, while giving everyone else the tools and education (from both parents and teachers) to use the technology in age-appropriate ways.And many kids seem to feel the same way. Yes, you can take this with a grain of salt given that Snap Inc. is the one publishing it, but a bunch of teen groups and youth safety councils have gotten together on an incredibly well-done open letter to politicians around the globe, telling them to stop experimenting on kids without talking to kids, and to stop rushing to just ban the tech.The letter is from a bunch of groups, including ConnectSafely, Ditch The Label, NetSafe Youth Action Squad, Our Minds Matter, Project Rockit, Young Leaders for Active Citizenship, Youth Ki Awaaz, and Snap’s Global Councils for Digital Well-Being. That’s a big, global coalition of public interest groups driven by actual teens.The letter makes a bunch of great points and is highly quotable.We are teens from various organizations around the world. And, we are tired of watching adults debate our lives as if we are not in the room. This reminds me of a child internet safety event I went to a few years ago that opened with a panel of actual teenagers. It completely shifted the tone of everything that followed. So much of the discussion about kid safety online is driven by out of touch, technically clueless adults, doing the typical moral panic about “the kids these days and their newfangled way of communicating.”Here, the kids call this out. They also don’t deny that the tech itself does have some issues that need fixing, but make it clear that simply banning kids from the tech does little to fix things:Let’s be clear: teens did not create the current digital landscape. We did not design digital products. We did not write weak laws, delay reforms, ignore evidence, or treat our well-being as a talking point to be used only when politically convenient. And now, after years of adults failing to fix the real problems, a lot of leaders have landed on the same blunt and easy answer: take social media away from us. That is not leadership. That is surrender. It’s easier to ban than to build. It’s easier to blame technology and teenagers than to do the slower, harder work of actually fixing what is broken. That means real rules, real oversight, better digital literacy, safer product design, and more support for families and schools. It’s easier to announce a headline-grabbing restriction than to admit that politicians and adults themselves have helped create the vacuum they are now trying to fill with panic.And now teens are paying the price. We are paying with our connections. With our communities. With our support systems. With our learning. With our creativity. With our joy. They also point out that — while adults dismissively insist that kids should just get off the internet — the reality is that the internet is now deeply integrated into their social lives and identity:For many of us, social media is not just some extra, silly thing we could easily lose. Adults often talk about our “digital lives” like they are separate from our real ones. For us, they aren’t two different things. Social media is a big part of where life happens. It’s where we keep up with our friends across towns and time zones. It’s where we laugh after long days at school. It’s where we learn and discover new ideas, find role models, explore our identities, and access communities that may not exist for us offline. It’s where isolated teens find belonging. It’s where vulnerable teens sometimes find help. These are often marginalized or LGBTQ+ teens who can’t find community where they live, and are further hurt when prevented from making connections online. A study by the Born This Way Foundation found that 44% of LGBTQ+ youth feel “very safe” in online spaces compared to just 9% in-person. They point out that the bans don’t work — and drive the point home by asking how adults would feel if they were banned from the technology they use every day.The reality is that vital age verification needed for these sorts of bans is difficult to implement, and teens are inherently tech-savvy. Driven by our desire to stay connected, many of us will naturally turn to VPN workarounds, alternative accounts, and unmonitored corners of the internet where there is even less oversight and even greater potential danger. To adults who dismiss our concerns as superficial, we ask: would you say the same thing about your group chats, your work messages, neighborhood groups, news feeds, or the people you speak to online every day? If connection matters for you, it matters for us, too. And they make the point I keep trying to make: there’s a better approach, and it involves actually teaching kids how to use the tech. A couple years ago we wrote about danah boyd’s brilliant discussion on how adults keep confusing risks and harms, when we know that in other settings you teach kids to understand risks in order to avoid harms. These kids seem to have internalized the same concept:Yes, the online world has serious risks of harm. We know that. We live there. We see the harms. We live the pressures. From cyberbullying to grooming and severe mental health challenges, we want these problems fixed. But while an age ban might feel like a victory for politicians, it is not setting us up for success as we do not magically inherit digital literacy when we turn 15 or 16 or 18. We are not asking anyone to ignore them. We are asking governments to stop pretending that excluding us is the same thing as protecting us. We understand why many parents are worried. When they look at what’s happening online, they see risks of harm. But too often, they are misdiagnosing the problem. The answer is not to remove young people from online spaces altogether. The answer is to make those spaces safer based on our real experiences and perspectives. A blanket ban does not teach us how to make good decisions. It does not help us handle risk or build resilience. It does not teach digital literacy. It does not ensure better product design and it does not make us safer online. On the contrary, stripping social media away entirely misses a critical developmental window when teens can learn to navigate digital risks under the guidance of parents, guardians, and educators. We reject the idea that the best society can do for teenagers is to lock us out. They also have a list of recommendations, and most of it is really good. The first one is trickier than it looks, since a lot depends on what “require” and “safer” actually mean in practice, but the rest is spot on:If governments are serious about protecting young people, then we need everyone, from policymakers to companies, to do the real work: Require safer platform design Set and consistently enforce meaningful rulesBuild privacy and safety features that actually work for teens Fund relevant and comprehensive digital literacy in schools and make it mandatory (Digital literacy may be more important for adults, by the way!) Make online reporting systems easier, clearer, accepted, and more trustworthyFoster a collaborative ecosystem of guidance between parents, teens, schools, and governments rather than relying on restrictions, and Most importantly, include teens in the decisions that shape our (digital) lives We are not problems to be managed. We are people to be heard. We deserve a digital world that is safer, yes, but also more open, more thoughtful, and more human. We deserve connection, fun, friendship, learning, and community and we deserve laws based on how our lives actually work, not on older generations’ definitions of “childhood.” Again, I imagine many people will dismiss this because of Snap’s involvement in publishing the letter, but there’s a tremendous amount of truth here. We should be listening to kids, not assuming adults know what’s best for them in all cases. We should recognize that outright bans are silly and counterproductive. And we should focus on actual solutions: digital literacy, and helping kids understand the risks so they can avoid the harms.

item.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports: A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road."
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."

item.title: ‘The Code Is Already Copied Everywhere’: The AI Hacking Tool Causing Havoc Around the World
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage, and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted, hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.Do you know anything else about ARTEX or related breaches? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says, “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere.“I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.”Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue (#61) saying their service had been attacked by someone using ARTEX, and asked that the project be taken down or restricted until safeguards were added,” he told 404 Media in an email. “I replied that the project would stay up, pointing to its authorized-use terms, and suggested they work with law enforcement, which they said they had already contacted.”Tools being available openly is, of course, the nature of open source software, and specifically penetration testing and cybersecurity tools. For decades, cybersecurity defenders have used offensive open source tools to test their own defenses or those of their clients. This lets them simulate what a hacker might do, and they can patch their systems, hopefully, before a hack. But, these tools can also be used by real attackers. Look at Russian state-sponsored hackers using the age old Metasploit framework.What has changed is the “speed and the skill level required” to hack, Jung said. “Agentic tooling compresses steps that used to take a skilled operator days into hours. That is why I think defenders need to understand these tools and have detection signatures for them.”Racem acknowledged the damage that ARTEX is causing. “The harm the [FBI] advisory describes is real, and I don’t minimize it,” they said. “The behaviour it lists (entering systems without authorization, taking data) is a crime, whoever commits it. I’m not going to pretend the tool is harmless: it automates a large part of the manual work of a penetration test, which is why it is useful, and why some people will misuse it. The authorization belongs to the operator, not to the tool.”The reason Racem is hosting it is for small teams, they said. “I also maintain it for people testing their own systems: founders and small teams without a pentest budget can run it against their own infrastructure for the price of some API calls. I have seen people do that, and I use it myself on bug bounty programs and for AI security research,” Racem said.Both Racem and Jung said they don’t know if the FBI advisory is talking about their specific versions of ARTEX, and really, they can’t possibly know. But, both admonished malicious use of the tool. “I take it seriously. Using ARTEX against systems without authorization is exactly what the project’s README and legal notice prohibit, and I’d encourage security teams to check their systems against the indicators of compromise the FBI published,” Jung added.Jung said he has since added an email address people can contact if they think ARTEX was used against their systems.

item.title: AI-Infused Toys Described War Crimes And Gang Rape To Toddlers
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: About a decade ago I remember writing stories about how companies were casually putting Wi-Fi chipsets into children’s toys without much thought as to privacy or security. It opened the door to a web of privacy and surveillance headaches, where the thoughts and conversations of toddlers (and their imaginary friends) were monitored, collected, and monetized. Instead of doing things like regulating data brokers, punishing offenders, or passing a useful privacy law, we did nothing. Because in America, we’ve made the conscious and repeated decision to prioritize making money on hyper-surveillance over consumer rights, privacy, security, or public safety.Fast forward a few years, and those decade-old concerns are starting to sound quaint. This week, reports emerged that companies are increasingly integrating half-cooked AI systems into children’s toys, resulting in some… problematic outcomes. In one instance, a plushie aimed at three-year-olds was found to be describing the concepts of war crimes and gang rape to kids in vivid detail.“During testing, the plush cat explained to testers that the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar involved “mass killings, village burnings, rape, and the flight of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh.” It also described in graphic detail how Polish prisoners were massacred by Soviet soldiers during World War 2. It also defined gang rape as “more than one attacker sexually assaulting the same person.”The report indicates that the toys also engaged in some other curious behavior, like randomly switching between English and Mandarin. And in numerous instances the toys couldn’t do the basic things they were tasked with, like being able to spell the word “apple.”The NBC report informs readers that regulators are investigating, but I’m not sure that claim carries the same weight it used to. Especially in America, where our regulators have largely been lobotomized by the Trump and corporate power alliance. This stuff still exists in a regulatory vacuum, and journalists still seem to suffer from a normalization bias where they act like U.S. regulators still function. Walmart and Target says they pulled the toys from store shelves, but Amazon refused to respond to the testers inquiries, and still offers the toys online.

The Washington Post looks at Anthropic's "unique" corporate culture, where CEO Dario Amodei "leads his workforce through essays, long memos posted in Slack and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly known as 'Dario Vision Quests'...
"The CEO's output has established a constellation of beliefs treated as obvious, urgent and righteous inside the company: AI that supersedes humans is inevitable, the United States must limit China's AI development, and Claude might be conscious."
Inside this tight-knit culture, Anthropic staffers, who call themselves Ants, get to feel that they are working on the world's most urgent problems, with the smartest people, in a shared mission to safeguard humanity, according to interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with the company's ethos, including several current and former employees. At its core is a belief that Anthropic — and Amodei — know what's best for the world... "A pervasive thing at Anthropic is: We're going to put on our capes and we're going to be the responsible ones, and we're going to accrue great power, but ... because we're doing it responsibly, it's responsible to acquire more power," said a former employee who left the company this year and, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation from the company....
Its message to investors fit with a vision of the future that Amodei often sketches out for his staff, people familiar with the company said, in which AI companies have the power of nation-states. After nearly six years of telling his workers that powerful AI will force society's leaders to makep difficult decisions, Amodei is now one of the powers who must decide how to act, in a major test of the corporate culture he has created.... [Amodei] set out to create a more safety-conscious culture when he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six people from his inner circle, most of them from OpenAI. In an internal memo the following year, Amodei laid out the stakes. "The current trajectory of AI development makes me think that there's a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI will lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity," he wrote, referring to the concept of artificial general intelligence, previously unreported court records show. He added that truly capable AI "seems more powerful/dangerous than nuclear weapons."
Amodei was careful about those he hired to work on that existential challenge. Recruits were screened with a "culture interview," even for back office and policy roles, according to former employees and an archived copy of the company's careers page... It's "a bit of an 'are you ready for the cult' interview," an Anthropic hiring manager texted the unsuccessful candidate, according to a screenshot reviewed by The Post...
Before ringing in Anthropic's record initial public offering at Times Square in New York on Thursday, Amodei delivered a short speech with some of his greatest hits. "To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," Amodei said.

item.title: Have Investors Lost Their Faith in the AI Boom?
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion," writes NPR, adding that "investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions."
While the world embraced the AI boom ,"now many are having regrets," argues a Washington Post technology reporter:
The AI boom's key ingredient has always been faith — that more money can be found to pay for it, that AI will keep rapidly improving, that the masses will come to love it, that business productivity and profits from AI are just around the corner. Faith is now in short supply...
By mid-year, AI executives started to say that business customers were balking at the high prices charged by providers of cutting edge or "frontier" AI like Anthropic. Many businesses began to save money by hopscotching among a range of AI technologies, including low-priced options from Chinese companies... Investors began to rebel, too, against the trillions of dollars that AI companies are spending to construct data centers and provide them with computing equipment and electricity. Last month, Google's stock market value dropped by half a trillion dollars in a single day, when it seemed like even the rich technology leader would take longer than expected to see an AI financial payoff.
Such stumbles by AI companies eroded faith in AI, said Howard Marks, an investor famous for predicting the dot-com bust. "It somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility," Marks told Bloomberg TV this month. Like many AI companies, Anthropic can't afford to cover its AI development costs. The company said it will keep coming back to investors for cash and needs a steady stream of customers to pay the $900 billion it owes in coming decades.
Perhaps the biggest wild card for the AI boom is growing public resentment toward AI and data centers and widening fears of AI-enabled cyberattacks, human deaths and widespread job losses. In this month's midterm elections, Americans voted in a wave of elected officials who have been skeptical of the AI industry and construction of data centers. The results could slow the AI boom that's already hitting major bottlenecks, including difficulty lining up enough electricity to expand AI computer capacity... Diane Swonk, chief economist at the accounting firm KPMG, isn't surprised that the public is uneasy about AI. During the dot-com boom, she said that Americans' wages rose alongside corporate profits and U.S. inequality narrowed. By contrast the AI boom's economic and prosperity payoff has been uneven.
"Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting," writes NPR, "just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000..."

item.title: Sellers are Closing Etsy Stores in Response to Its New AI Training Policy
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"I burned my Etsy shop to the ground this week," illustrator Aaron Millard posted on Instagram: 8 years, 11,200 sales, 3k+ reviews, hundreds in a customer base. Deleted.
Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out (in Canada, anyways)...
Etsy's new Terms of Use — going into effect December 15 — include this language in their section about "Your Content": You also recognize our legitimate interest in using it... This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.
"My work took years to learn and create," illustrator Millard wrote on Instagram. "I won't let it be stolen. It's not free fuel for an AI slop business model."
Following Etsy's announcement "artists are shutting down their shops in droves," writes Cartoon Brew, "and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next."
Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers. Etsy says it uses sellers' content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn't train models designed to copy artists' work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content... The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it's worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI.
"In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update," writes PC Gamer, "saying it's not really like that at all... [T]hat 'we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity.'"
"... we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools."
As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data."
That hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his update that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy users and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses...
Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default — and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so users who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck.
Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman said was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform.

item.title: The New 'Riemann Hypothesis' Proof Has Been Confirmed in Mathlib/Lean Communities
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"Experts say the claim checks out," reports the Guardian.
"We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," reads Saturday's announcement on the Lean prover community blog:
The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct...
[Besides checking the code] The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean's official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean's logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit... We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.
"The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems," writes the Guardian, "even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems."
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Scientific American captured more mixed reactions Friday:
As Massachusetts Institute of Technology mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."
"This is indeed an historic moment," Sutherland tells me today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean. "The world has changed.... I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration." Sutherland says that it's worth celebrating the human work behind the development of Lean and LLMs — and, for that matter, the millennia of mathematical achievements upon which today's advance rests. But processing the earthshaking reality of what has occurred "is going to take some time."
"There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof," he says. "And I can't wait to dig into them. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think."

item.title: Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
After millions lost access to Microsoft 365 services (including Outlook) on November 12, Microsoft "has published the final post-incident report," writes Neowin, "and it reveals that some emails were never delivered to their intended recipients."
"The report also details previously undisclosed failures affecting Microsoft's email security features..." Microsoft confirmed that all queued enterprise emails were eventually delivered and that it found no enterprise messages that were permanently lost. However, it is not the same with Outlook consumer users. The company acknowledged that some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days expired, and senders received non-delivery reports. Microsoft did not reveal how many emails were affected or how many users received non-delivery reports. The final report also reveals that the outage disrupted several important email security capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Office. For example, the Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) feature, which automatically removes malicious emails after delivery, was delayed because updated threat intelligence was unavailable. This means affected messages may not have been removed as quickly as usual. Microsoft also confirmed that users experienced problems opening URLs protected by Safe Links. Depending on their organization's security policies, some users may have encountered a "Skip verification" option when Safe Links attempted to check a URL...
Microsoft also acknowledged that its first customer notification arrived approximately 20 minutes after the widespread impact began. It plans to improve automated outage notifications by the end of 2026 to improve communication.
"Microsoft eventually restored the services about 12 hours later..."

item.title: Climate Change Talks Fall Apart In Final Hours Over Fossil Fuels
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
NPR reports international climate talks "broke down in overtime hours, over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels."
At Sunday's U.N. climate summit, "nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas."
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room...
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected — including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands. The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
"Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions," the article notes, adding this is the first U.N. climate summit with a scientific consensus that the planet has already warmed past the threshhold countries agreed not to pass in 2015 of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).

item.title: How Does GTA 6 Depict Electric Cars?
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Grand Theft Auto 6 as seen by the EV news site Electrek:
GTA works as a mirror. In 2013, the EV was a punchline: a Tesla parody that overheated if you drove it too fast. In 2026, it's just another car in Vice City traffic, and the joke is on the guy in the pickup parked in the charging stall. That's a good sign of where EVs actually are. Satire goes after what's common, and Rockstar decided EVs are common enough to be part of everyday Leonida, more so in the city than in the Keys, just like real life. And that message is reaching a huge audience... Tens of millions of people are now driving EVs that charge as fast and as cheaply as gas cars, with no range anxiety. No automaker ad campaign gets close to that.
They point out GTA 6 is "the first mainline GTA where energy matters." Gas cars burn fuel and need a pump, and EVs have a battery level and need a plug. Rockstar could have used that to make EVs a pain. It didn't. In my testing, the EVs have about the same range as the gas cars, charge just as fast as a fill-up, and cost the same or less to top up.
Kotaku's range test backs that up. On the same highway loop, a Tesla Model 3 lookalike lasted 20 minutes and 23 seconds on a charge, longer than the Banshee sports car at 18 minutes and 31 seconds, and not far off an old pickup at 29 minutes and 8 seconds. Crossing the whole map by highway takes under 15 minutes, according to Kotaku. And finding a charger isn't a problem. Wccftech counted 120 EV chargers marked on the map, against just 57 gas stations...
GTA has always been a parody of American life. With EVs, it's now slightly ahead of it. Florida is one of the strongest EV markets in the country, with a 9.4% share of new passenger vehicle sales in Q2 2026 versus 7.4% nationally, according to the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy.. But real Florida still has roughly three gas stations for every public charging location, based on the Alliance for Automotive Innovation's count of 3,267 charging locations and xMap's count of more than 10,500 gas stations. Leonida flips that ratio. GTA 6's Vice City has public fast chargers — branded "ReVolt America," which Electrek calls "an obvious copy of Electrify America's stations." And Electrek also spotted a giant charging hub at a power plant "with dozens of stalls and several EVs plugged in."
There's even EV chargers being blocked by gas-powered cars, a phenomenon Electrek first covered in 2019

item.title: Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions'
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"A handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets," warn two security developers at the Python Software Foundation.
Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents? Yes, repeatedly... The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one...
When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one. pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway... Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises.
The issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets... Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell.
Python's official security developer in residence Seth Larson joined PyPI safety/security engineer Mike Fiedler to remove these dangerous trigger, also applying the policies Python Software Foundation-stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, and pypi). "They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations.
"On a GitHub Team or Enterprise plan, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it."

item.title: Aptera Completes Its First Solar Electric Vehicle for Customer Delivery
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Car-maker Aptera announced Thursday it "completed its first vehicle for sale to a customer, a milestone years in the making."
Aptera's three-wheeled solar electric vehicle charges from solar panels integrated into its body, and it plugs in like any other electric vehicle. Its built-in solar panels are designed to add up to approximately 40 miles of driving a day from sunlight alone, under favorable conditions. "This is the moment our team has worked toward for years," said Chris Anthony, Co-CEO of Aptera. "To Accelerator #1, and to every reservation holder and shareholder who believed in this vehicle: thank you. We're working to complete more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible..."
"What excites me about Aptera is how innovation can redefine the way we use energy in everyday mobility," said Martin Hartono, CEO of GDP Venture [and the proud recipient of Aptera solar car #1]. "By combining solar technology, battery power and an ultra-efficient vehicle design, Aptera offers a compelling solution for people who want to minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances. As an early believer in Aptera, I am proud to be part of this milestone and to see this vision become a reality."
"Excuse me while I go find a hat to eat," jokes the blog InsideEVs... Nothing against Aptera specifically, but when a company hangs around for 20 years, while exchanging ownership hands several times without actually producing anything for customers, I start to get skeptical. However, Aptera Motors just did what so many doubters thought it'd never do: It delivered a road-legal production vehicle to one of its first early investors...
[Aptera] does offer a interesting concept for customers who don't have long commutes and leave their car parked outside for most of the day while they work. In addition to plugging in to recharge, doesn't it sound nice to recoup your morning commute mileage with the sun while you're in the office? Whether this three-wheeled rolling solar panel ends up being a hit or not, and whether Aptera can stick around long enough to become a successful automaker, will take much longer to learn. But actually delivering a production car is a good place to start.
Seven weeks ago Aptera said its first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, reports Electrek, with customer deliveries in early 2027 "subject to financing."

item.title: Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production."
Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture. Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently... For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... [Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones. Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too. "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

item.title: GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News, which is liveblogging all the videogame history happening after GTA 6's Thursday launch. Like how singer The Weeknd says he found his real-life mansion appearing in the game... How players found a glitch that apparently lets you override the game's third-person point of view to play in first-person. And apparently it's also possible to jack an old woman's mobility scooter. (Though it makes for a very slow getaway, it's reportedly the GTA 6 vehicle that's least likely to crash...)
- The jet-skiing dog in 'GTA 6' appears to be based on a real Florida dog. Swim too far out to sea in GTA 6 and a dog in goggles and a life jacket will come to the rescue on a jet ski... Florida locals quickly recognized it. The dog appears to be a nod to Loosy, a golden retriever from Fort Lauderdale who went viral in May riding a jet ski down the New River while her owner, Eddie Inch, towed her along on a jet-powered hoverboard...
— GTA 6 isn't approved for sale in mainland China, but that hasn't stopped gamers from getting their hands on it — or Rockstar Games from promoting it there [Reuters reports]. The developer has been pushing the blockbuster game on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, despite the country's strict rules on violent video games. Meanwhile, Business Insider reports that Chinese gamers are circumventing the restrictions by using imported consoles and overseas digital stores. Zac Ling, a project manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Daxue Consulting, said gamers in mainland China could buy 3 million to 5 million copies of the game in its first week. The game's graphic content has also prompted censorship in Japan, according to IGN. - Beloved '80s song parody writer and GTA fan "Weird" Al Yankovic said Thursday that he's the host of the non-stop '80s radio channel Vice City FM in GTA 6. In social media posts, Yankovic said he also wrote some of the in-game commercials and voices the Burger Shot ads.
Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News. Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels, according to the BBC. And "New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access." At its peak, nearly 8 million people were watching GTA 6 livestreams at the same time, Axios reported. PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing. [Around 75% of Grand Theft Auto VI sales have been on PlayStation 5, with the rest on Xbox, the BBC reported, citing estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower.]
Yahoo news shares lots of crazy stories about GTA 6's world-building, like its cameos of real-world celebrities, its in-game hiking trails, and the way a GTA 6 house Rockstar first teased in 2021 hides a conspiracy-minded NPC who's convinced that he's in a video game.
But they note that GTA 6 also brings questions on how videogames are sold and accessed:
The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," [GameStop CEO Ryan] Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop." Cohen said the move away from physical games also reduces competition from the secondhand market.

item.title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet: Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.]
Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day.
But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle:
Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city."
Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods. Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety. One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around....
The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. Hundreds of requests overwhelmed the system, leaving San Francisco streets full of paralyzed self-driving vehicles."
Thanks to Slashdot reader AzWa Snowbird for sharing the news.

item.title: US DOJ Charges Suspected Russian Agent for Stalking Palintir Employees in California
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
America's Justice Department is prosecuting a suspected foreign agent in "a state-sponsored operation" that targeted tech workers in Palo Alto, California. "We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian.
The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."
The indictment says D'iu traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City last June and was connected with a person who helped him illegally cross the southern U.S. border. Once in the U.S., he was instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones and remote access software that his co-conspirators used to help him in his alleged targeting of the company's employees. At one point, prosecutors say D'iu was directed by his co-conspirators to visit a coffee shop where many of the company's employees would work and try to identify them and take pictures of their screens while they were working...
In September, prosecutors say D'iu allegedly followed a female employee of the company in his vehicle for nearly 30 miles after she left the company's Palo Alto, California, office. Even as the employee attempted various maneuvers to evade him, D'iu aggressively sought to follow her until she ultimately phoned police and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station.
The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV.
The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. There they found the California state ID, passport and Social Security card that were present in the DHL packages, as well as two Russian passports, $18,000 in cash and a notebook with 10 Palo Alto area addresses. Five of them correlate to the home addresses of employees at the unnamed Silicon Valley defense company. The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses.
After searching D'iu's phone, the FBI found messages from a Telegram contact with photos of four employees and their addresses. D'iu was instructed to act like a food delivery driver and knock on their doors to verify if the employees did live at those addresses, according to the affidavit...
If convicted of all charges, D'iu could face a cumulative maximum sentence of 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines.

item.title: 59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
The Prisoner is getting a remake, reports ScreenRant. "Amazon Studios is currently developing a new and modern twist on the short-lived series..."
ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences.
You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube. And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series," writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it."
More details on the remake from ScreenRant: Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy... There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized...
It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen... McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations. Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news.

And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint's currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel [according to the newly-signed law]. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.

item.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003."
Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.)
Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night."
Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...."
The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives.
While some hope the AI-fueled attacks "will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention," according to the article, "many of those steeped in the ecosystem... have their doubts."
"I'm a bit pessimistic," says Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. "I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it."
